blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Look up. That big gray cloud is a storm. Watch. A flash. The whole sky goes white for one blink. That flash is lightning. It is a giant spark. Then you hear it. Boom. That noise is thunder. Light is fast, so you see the flash first. Sound is slow, so the boom comes after. Count with me. One. Two. Three. The storm is far away. You are safe inside.

blocks.prompt: Where the Bang Comes From
blocks.text: Lightning is a giant spark. It is made inside a tall storm cloud. High up in that cloud it is freezing cold. Tiny bits of ice bump into each other all day long. All that bumping makes the cloud electric. It is a little like rubbing your socks on a rug and then touching a doorknob. When the cloud holds too much, a spark jumps out. The spark is so hot that it makes the air blow up. The air shoves out hard in every direction. That shove is the sound you hear. That is thunder. Light is fast. Sound is slow. So the flash always comes first, and the boom comes after.

blocks.prompt: Why the Sky Bangs
blocks.text: Inside a thunderstorm, air rushes upward fast enough to carry a hailstone. Up there it is freezing. Ice crystals and lumps of soft hail crash into each other over and over. Every crash rubs a little electric charge off one and onto the other, and slowly the cloud splits in two. The light crystals ride the wind to the top and carry a positive charge. The heavy hail sinks to the bottom and carries a negative charge. Air normally blocks electricity. It will not let it through. But if the charge builds up high enough, the air gives up. A path tears open between the cloud and the ground, and a huge spark rips down it. That spark is lightning. The spark is only about as wide as your thumb, but it heats the air around it to nearly 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit. That is roughly five times hotter than the surface of the sun. Air that hot cannot sit still. It explodes outward, slams into the cool air around it, and that shove travels to your ears as a long rumble. The rumble is thunder. Light reaches you almost instantly. Sound crawls, taking about five seconds to cross one mile. So count the seconds after a flash, divide by five, and you have just measured the storm.

blocks.prompt: The Ladder of Light
blocks.text: A lightning flash does not simply appear. It gets built, in stages, and the whole construction takes less time than a blink. It starts inside a thundercloud that has torn itself into layers of charge. Rising air carries light ice crystals to the top, where they collect a positive charge. Heavier pellets of soft, slushy hail, called graupel, sink toward the base and collect a negative charge. The cloud is now an enormous battery, and the ground below it turns positive in answer. When that imbalance grows strong enough, a faint, forked channel called a stepped leader begins to feel its way down out of the cloud. It moves in jerks of about fifty yards at a time, branching, pausing, choosing. It is almost too dim to notice. As the leader nears the ground, the ground reaches back. Streamers of positive charge lift from fence posts, trees, steeples, anything tall and handy. When one streamer touches the leader, the circuit closes. Electricity floods back up the finished channel at about one third the speed of light, and that surge, called the return stroke, is the blinding flash you actually see. It carries roughly thirty thousand amps. Often the cloud is not done. It fires again down the same channel, three or four times in a few tenths of a second, which is why lightning seems to flicker. Most flashes never reach the ground at all. They jump inside a cloud or between clouds, lighting the storm from within like a lamp in fog. Only about one flash in four comes down to touch the Earth. Those are the ones we photograph, and they are the reason a tall building wears a metal rod on its roof.

blocks.prompt: The Storm That Wires Itself
blocks.text: Every second, somewhere on Earth, the sky flashes about forty times. Satellites watch it happen. From orbit, the planet looks like it is quietly blinking. Lightning begins with a problem of balance. Inside a tall storm cloud, air rushes upward at highway speed through a zone colder than a freezer. Ice crystals and graupel, which are soft pellets of half frozen slush, collide there millions of times. Each collision strips a small charge off one and hands it to the other. The light crystals ride the updraft to the top of the cloud carrying positive charge. The heavy graupel sinks, taking negative charge down with it. Physicists still argue about the fine detail of that exchange, but the result is not in doubt. The cloud separates into stacked layers of opposite charge, and it does so with staggering force. Air is a good insulator. It refuses to carry electricity until it is pushed far past its limit. A thundercloud pushes it there. The air tears open, and a dim, branching stepped leader gropes downward in jerks. Streamers rise to meet it from anything tall. The moment they touch, an enormous return stroke rips back up the channel at a third of the speed of light, carrying around thirty thousand amps and heating a column of air narrower than your wrist to roughly fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit. That is about five times the temperature of the sun's surface. Air cannot be heated that violently and stay still. It detonates outward, and the shock wave rolls away as thunder. For most of human history the flash was simply divine. Then, in May 1752, a French scientist named Thomas-Francois Dalibard planted a tall iron rod in a garden outside Paris, following a plan published by Benjamin Franklin, and drew sparks out of a passing storm. The sky, it turned out, ran on the same electricity as a jar on a laboratory bench. Franklin took the discovery one step further and gave the world the lightning rod, a piece of metal whose only job is to offer the strike an easy, boring path into the ground. That is the quiet genius of it. You cannot argue with thirty thousand amps. You can only give them somewhere to go.

6.title: The Spark That Splits the Sky
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Spark That Splits the Sky

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Roughly 100 million volts between cloud base and ground
Stepped leader: jerks of about fifty yards
Return stroke: about one third the speed of light
Fulgurite: sand fused into a glass tube
Sprites and blue jets flicker above the storm
The Empire State Building takes about 20 hits a year
Dalibard ran Franklin's experiment in May 1752

blocks.prompt: The Sky's Short Circuit
blocks.text: Lightning is the most familiar thing on Earth that nobody can fully explain. Start with what is solid. A thunderstorm is a machine for lifting water. Warm, damp air rises, cools, and condenses, and the heat released by that condensing drives it higher still, until a single storm cloud can stand ten miles tall and hold the weight of a small mountain in water. In the freezing middle of that column, two kinds of ice meet. Small crystals drift upward on the updraft. Larger pellets of soft, slushy ice, called graupel, are heavy enough to fall against it. They collide, endlessly, and each collision leaves the crystal a little more positive and the graupel a little more negative. The updraft then does the sorting: positives to the top, negatives to the base. Exactly why the collisions divide the charge this way is still being worked out in laboratories. The storm does not wait for the paperwork. What it builds is a capacitor the size of a town, holding a difference of perhaps a hundred million volts between its base and the ground. Air resists this. Air is an insulator, and a good one, which is the only reason the atmosphere is not permanently on fire. But every insulator has a breaking point, and the storm walks the air straight past it. The failure begins as a stepped leader: a dim, forked channel of torn air that gropes downward from the cloud in jerks of about fifty yards, pausing, branching, searching. It is not aiming. It is simply following whichever patch of air happens to give way next. As it descends, the ground beneath it grows positive, and streamers of upward charge lift from trees, masts, fence wire, and the tops of tall buildings, straining toward it. The strike happens when one streamer and the leader touch. In that instant the circuit closes, and the return stroke, the flash you actually see, surges back up the completed channel at roughly one third the speed of light. Thirty thousand amps pour through a channel of air about as wide as your thumb, and it reaches near fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit, roughly five times the heat of the sun's own surface. Air that hot does not glow politely. It explodes, and the shock wave of that explosion, rolling and bouncing off clouds and hills, is thunder. The consequences run further than the noise. Lightning is hot enough to rip nitrogen molecules apart in mid air, and the fragments fall to the ground in rain as nitrate, a fertilizer the sky makes for free. Strike a beach and the sand can fuse into a fulgurite, a rough glass tube shaped like the bolt's own path. Above the storm, faint red sprites and blue jets flicker upward toward space, unnoticed until pilots kept reporting them and a camera finally caught one in 1989. The old fears deserve a correction too. Lightning strikes the same place constantly: the Empire State Building takes around twenty hits a year, which is precisely what a lightning rod is for. A car is safe not because of its rubber tires, which are irrelevant, but because its metal shell carries the current around the people inside. Roughly nine out of ten people struck in the United States survive, though many do not walk away unchanged. Benjamin Franklin sketched the experiment. Thomas-Francois Dalibard ran it first, in a French garden in May 1752, drawing from a passing cloud the same sparks a laboratory could make on demand. That was the end of the thunderbolt as a weapon of the gods and the beginning of it as a circuit. Two and a half centuries later we can time a strike to the microsecond and film the leader as it feels its way down. We still cannot tell you, exactly, how the ice does it.
